title_en: The Best Controllers for Playing PC Games in 2026 - IGN
summary_en: You don't have to use a mouse and keyboard if you don't want to.
body_en:
After spending several weeks testing 30 of the PC controllers, the Flydigi Vader 5 Pro stands out for its clicky mechanical buttons, long-lasting battery, and Hall-Effect thumbsticks whose tension you can adjust at any time.
But players who want a symmetrical stick layout or a pad built for large hands should look elsewhere.
I'm a journalist with more than 12 years of experience writing about games and reviewing hardware. I play most of my games on PC, and I switch between mouse input and a controller depending on what I'm playing. I rotate through several PC controllers every year, from brands big and small, and have a good sense of the strengths and weaknesses of different manufacturers.
Away from PC, I play my Nintendo Switch and Xbox Series S with controllers, often third-party devices that are compatible with PC.
To pick the best controller for PC gaming, I first compiled a longlist of potential pads that I thought had a shot. I then cut that down to a shortlist and tested everything on it, arriving at a handful of recommendations.
When I began this process I didn't have a concrete blueprint in mind for the best controller, but I knew what attributes I wanted.
I wanted controllers with reliable, tactile face buttons – but I didn't care whether they were clicky and mechanical or the more traditional, softer-feel "membrane" buttons. I wanted accurate, long-lasting sticks, ideally with Hall Effect or Tunnel Magnetoresistance (TMR) sensors that use magnets rather than physical contacts, and are therefore less prone to wear and "stick drift.” I wanted smooth triggers, a comfortable shape, a bouncy D-Pad for navigating menus or playing arcade-style games, and a battery life of 6-8 hours at an absolute minimum, but ideally much longer.
I had an extra set of features that I considered non-essential, but nice to have. These included a headphone jack, customization software, a charging dock, and extra remappable buttons on the controller, for flexibility (so you can, for example, remap fiddly control-stick clicks to the more reliable press of a button.)
I considered both wired and wireless pads, preferring wireless when possible for their flexibility.
Using this criteria, I assembled a longlist of controllers for potential recommendation. From my own experience, I had a sense of what I wanted to test and the manufacturers I would focus on, but to broaden my search I read critic reviews – across IGN, hardware-focused outlets, and user opinions, mostly on controller subreddits. I scoured existing lists of best controllers and noted any devices that repeatedly cropped up. I watched hours of YouTube videos where hardware reviewers and enthusiasts ranked their own lists or analysed popular controllers.
I avoided leaning on any individual source. Instead, I used all these sources to better understand the controller landscape, both budget and high-end, and to list any I thought had even an outside shot of being among the best.
After this exercise my longlist stretched to around 40 controllers, and I wanted a maximum of about 25 controllers to ensure I had sufficient time with each one. To make cuts, I dove deeper into user and critic tests, looking for common flaws or quality-control complaints in my longlisted products, trimming any that persistently had issues (such as the Flydigi Apex 4.) I checked the availability of each controller, losing any that were no longer in production, had been superseded by more recent controllers, or were particularly tricky to get hold of.
At this point I also picked my categories, which helped me trim the list further. I knew I wanted a single recommendation that would work for most people – but I also wanted a budget pick, a budget wireless option, and a classy, high-budget pick. From my research, I also decided I needed a symmetrical-stick option for those who preferred the Dualsense-style layout, and a controller for larger hands (controllers feeling too small was a common complaint). I eliminated controllers that didn't easily fit into my categories.
Once I had my shortlist, I requested the controllers from manufacturers and began testing. I couldn't get hold of a few controllers on my shortlist: EasySMX declined to send three shortlisted controllers, Asus couldn't get two controllers to me, Microsoft couldn't send the Xbox Elite Series 2 Controller (but did send the base Xbox controller), and I wasn't sent one Razer controller.
You can tell a lot about a controller before even switching it on. I spent five to ten minutes with each pad out of the box, pressing each button and squeezing each trigger.
I was checking that they all worked flawlessly – that they didn't stick or squeak – but I was also assessing how everything felt . Were they tactile, clicky, and satisfying to hit? Were they mushy, lifeless, and hollow-sounding? Was the controller comfortable to hold? Could I easily reach every input? Did the controller creak or bend when I pulled and twisted it?
Then, I began playing.
I put each controller through a line-up of games one-by-one. Not every controller made it through every game: if I could tell after half an hour that I wasn't going to recommend a controller – because it was uncomfortable or because its sticks felt spongy, for example – I eliminated it and picked up the next pad.
The games I tested:
I picked GTA 5 first because it essentially tests the controller in lots of genres at once: driving, shooting, running around on foot, and even using the D-Pad to navigate menus or your in-game phone. EA FC 26's quick, precise inputs tested control stick accuracy and button responsiveness, Marathon tested first-person aiming, platforming, and trigger speed, Celeste taxed the D-Pad, and Forza Horizon 5 let me focus on the triggers and pure left-to-right analogue accuracy.
For each game I asked myself, first, was the controller working as intended, with accurate, responsive inputs and no errors? And second: was I enjoying it? Did I like squeezing each trigger, could I spam face buttons quickly? Would I happily use this controller every day?
Playing for hours at a time gave me a sense of how comfortable each controller was to use. Whether a specific device fits your hand depends on their relative size (for reference, I have slightly larger-than-average hands for a man,) but I also looked up user reviews to see how comfortable they were for other people. I could also tell, after a few hours, how quickly a controller's battery was draining, and how that compared to manufacturers' claims.
When available I downloaded a controller's PC software and spent time within it, remapping buttons and fiddling with settings. I wanted to know how intuitive it was, how many options it housed, and whether it worked consistently. For example, did remapping the back button in the software translate to in-game presses?
I then looked for some more objective tests to complement my subjective assessments.
I tested each controller in Stick Tracer, an all-in-one tool for testing left and right sticks. It shows how far the sticks sit away from the center at rest, called "center error", as well as the exact shape of the extremities of your input and whether it deviates from a perfect circle, called "circle error". Its movement tracers could help me find inconsistencies, and it shows real-time polling rate to compare to a manufacturer's promises.
Latency itself – whether Bluetooth, wired, or via a USB dongle – is almost impossible to test reliably without extra, dedicated hardware. Thankfully, a website called Gamepadla aggregates and verifies user tests and is the go-to site for assessing latency. For every controller, I measured it by eye – could I detect any delay? Did it feel snappy? Was Bluetooth laggier than wired? But I also checked the Gamepadla pages for a more objective breakdown. I was looking for a latency of less than 20ms, and ideally less than 10.
I tested how quickly I could press each controller's buttons on ShmupSpeed, an online tool that measures your click rate. I tested one face button and one button for each controller, running each test three times to get an average, and noted down the results.
No one metric can tell you whether a controller is good: I tried to assess each one as a whole, using the numbers from Stick Tracer, Gamepadla and ShmupSpeed to supplement my hands-on tests.
The Vader 5 Pro has everything I want in a controller: a comfortable grippy body, tactile buttons, smooth triggers, tons of extra programmable inputs, a low-latency connection and a battery that can stretch way beyond 15 hours – all for $80. A spinning dial around the Hall Effect thumbsticks that adjusts their tension is a wonderful bonus that you won't find on many other controllers.
You can adjust stick tension whenever you want. Very few controllers let you tweak stick tension, and no controller does it as simply as the Vader 5 Pro. Just rotate the ridged ring around each stick, feeling the bump of each increment, to make them tighter or looser. The result is instant and the gap between the loosest and tightest settings is so vast that you're almost guaranteed to find something that works for you. I adjusted it game to game, tightening it for more precise aiming in Marathon, and loosening it for the more laissez-faire flicks of EA FC 26. Crucially, the sticks felt accurate and reliable no matter the tension, snapping back to the center whenever I let go.
Its buttons are clicky and respond instantly. I love the face buttons' crisp sound and feel. They're quick to spam and scored highly in ShmupSpeed, but I never hit one accidentally. The bumpers feel sleek, the back buttons are well-positioned and satisfyingly crunchy to squeeze, and the D-Pad tension feels just about perfect for Celeste's precise platforming. The extra two face buttons are cheap and stiff – but they're still nice to have, and besides, there are six other remappable buttons to pick from.
You can remap eight extra programmable buttons. That's more than almost any other controller I've encountered, and opens up new possibilities, particularly for first-person shooters where your thumbs are trying to aim and smash the face buttons at the same time. For Marathon I assigned all the face buttons to the extra buttons on the back, so I could freely jump, reload, switch weapons or crouch while still aiming with my right thumb. I then used the extra bumper buttons to mimic clicking the controller sticks in. I left the two extra face buttons unassigned, but I'm sure you could find a clever use for them.
Its blistering connection to its USB dongle is as fast as a wire. Its Bluetooth connection is okay, but the included 2.4 GHz dongle gives you a wireless connection that feels instant. Gamepadla results show latencies of less than 5ms for buttons and sticks. That's seriously fast, and means you can play wirelessly without sacrificing performance.
Its quick-press trigger mode feels particularly rapid. Like with many good controllers, the Vader 5 Pro can toggle between regular triggers that you pull through an arc and a short-travel mode that feels like a click. The physical switch to swap between the two modes slides easily, and the quick-pull triggers have the same snappiness as a quality mouse button. I used them for Marathon, and felt like they sped up my trigger finger.
Its battery lasts for ages. Plenty of controllers, including some on this list, can't make it to 10 hours. The Vader 5 Pro lasted roughly 15-18 hours for me, and you could stretch that further if you turn off the customizable RGB strip on the bottom of the controller, or reduce vibration. Some users report up to 25 hours of use. It's enough to get you through multiple long sessions.
Flydigi's software is deep and intuitive. I didn't have high hopes when I loaded it and saw the Chinese characters labelling my different profiles – but beyond that I found a system that's easy to use. Adjusting the lighting, remapping the buttons, and tweaking the joystick sensitivity curve and deadzones is simple, and you can even individually customize the vibration for the grips and each trigger. I tinkered until I found a setup I liked, and I occasionally tweaked it as I moved between games.
It's not a budget controller, but it's solid value. For $80, you're getting something that feels as good and performs as well as devices that are double the price.
GameSir's G7 Pro gets all the plaudits – but I prefer the more affordable Cyclone 2. Its face buttons are cleaner, its D-Pad simpler, and its TMR sticks feel just as good. It plays like a premium pad, but costs $50.
Its sticks are remarkable for a $50 pad. TMR tech is considered the gold standard for control sticks, and you won't find it on many controllers at this price. Gamesir's feel smooth, balanced, and responsive, with negligible centering error. I also love the thick, grippy ring atop the sticks to stop your thumb sliding off.
Face buttons feel premium, too. I enjoy the firm, sharp click they make. They're sensitive, spammable, and I never nudged them accidentally. They wiggle a little in place – something you won't find on the Vader 5 Pro, for example – but it's nothing dramatic, and never hurt me in-game. They actually feel better, to me, than those on the more expensive Gamesir G7 Pro, whose buttons occasionally squeaked as they rubbed against their casing.
A charging dock helps mitigate middling battery life. Again, few controllers at this price have a dock. The Cyclone 2 dock's barebones design means you have to place the controller in carefully, which is slightly annoying. But just by existing, it makes it more likely you'll charge the controller after a session – and that partially mitigates the average battery life of 6-10 hours. If you want to get as much juice out of it as possible, you can turn the RGB off and reduce the 1000Hz polling rate to 500Hz without taking any real noticeable hit in performance.
Its USB dongle connection is instant and reliable. I tested the GameSir in all three modes: wired, Bluetooth, and wireless via its USB dongle. The dongle is best – you'll find faster wireless connections on high-end pads, but the Cyclone 2 is still rapid, and I didn't notice any delay between my inputs and the in-game response. The dongle always recognised my controller instantly and the connection never dropped. Plus, I love how tiny the dongle is: you barely notice it sticking out of your PC or laptop, and you can store it in the charging dock for safekeeping.
Its crowd-pleasing shape will be comfortable for most people. Xbox's wireless controller is a tried and tested shape that fits most people, and the Cyclone 2's shape is nearly identical, down to the curve of the bumpers. I certainly found it comfortable to hold for hours at a time, no matter what genre I was playing, and my left thumb felt at home on its clicky D-Pad when playing Celeste. Whether you use one finger for the bumpers and triggers or two, you'll easily reach the two back buttons, one on each side of the controller.
GameSir's software all fits on one page. GameSir Connect controls the Cyclone 2, and I like that everything fits on a single screen. From there you can control RGB, change the polling rate, remap buttons, adjust the sticks and configure gyro controls. It's nothing revolutionary, but it feels streamlined.
It sticks aren't TMR but they feel better than anything I've ever used: tight, springy, and accurate, plus you can adjust the tension by removing the controller's face plate. All its buttons are solid and satisfyingly clicky, and its party trick is adaptive triggers that respond to your actions in games, ratcheting the tension up and down as you fire your gun or pulse the accelerator. A giant battery completes the package. It's $160, but it's worth it.
Its adaptive triggers are a genuine delight . In certain games, the triggers automatically adjust their tension to match your in-game actions: it's basically Flydigi's attempt to capture the joy of the Dualsense controller's triggers, and it's the best implementation you'll find outside of Sony's pad. It works in around 100 games and I enjoyed it most in GTA 5, where it changed when I was driving a car – increasing the resistance under braking or acceleration – or shooting a shotgun, which gave me a snap of breakthrough tension to mimic the gun firing, and then lots of recoil vibration. It's not perfect, and setting it up in FlyDigi's software isn't the most intuitive, but it genuinely makes games more fun. If your game is unsupported, you can still customize the trigger tension around five presets.
Sticks spring back to the center, and you can adjust the tension. These are, by far, the sticks I enjoyed the most. Not only are they smooth and responsive, but they fairly race back to dead center with a taught twang when you stop pushing them. They sit at dead center, with virtually zero deviation – their centering error was the lowest of the pads I tested. I also loved watching the mechanism twirl beneath the transparent face plate. On top of all that, you can adjust the tension. I wish it was easier: you have to first remove the faceplate and then twiddle a pair of tiny screws, but it's the kind of thing you can do once and then, when they're perfect for you, never do again.
Buttons all feel fantastic, including the six remappable ones. The tension on the face buttons is just right: you're rewarded for a firm press with a clear click and fast bounce, allowing you to hit it rapidly all over again. Its six remappable inputs – two near the bumpers, four on the back – are expertly placed so that you can press them whenever you want, and I never felt I was straining or stretching my fingers. On the back you get two buttons and two paddles. They're sensitive, to the point where I accidentally hit them when I began using the Apex 5, but I quickly adjusted.
Battery life is practically unbeatable for a high-end pad. Yes, you'll get more from a standard Xbox controller or a Switch Pro – but for premium controllers connecting to a dongle, its 20-30 hours is about as good as it gets. To hit the higher end, you'll want to turn off its RGB and the mini display.
An eye-catching, futuristic aesthetic. I don't normally go in for RGB or transparent peripherals, but the Apex 5 is, in my eyes, a looker. Its transparent faceplate, splashes of blue and RGB notes feel futuristic and unique without being obnoxious. The built-in colour screen lends further chances for colour, and you can loop an animation of your choosing. Looks are subjective, of course, but I'm smitten. Its heavier weight makes it feel luxurious in your hands, too.
The digital display is handy for remapping buttons. It's not just for looks: it houses a detailed settings menu that feels almost as powerful as Flydigi's standalone app. You can switch between adaptive trigger modes, adjust vibration levels, and remap buttons here, rather than having to minimize your game and open separate software. The only catch is that the menu, at least in my model, was set to Chinese out of the box, but I figured out how to change languages without hassle.
You can dive into Flydigi's software for more customization. It's the same tool powering the Vader 5 Pro, and it's equally deep for the Apex 5. Setting up the adaptive controllers for specific games was a little glitchy, and a couple of times the list of games vanished entirely, requiring me to restart the app. But that was the only hiccup.
Go in with eyes open: some users report quality-control problems. Every controller has defects for some people, including high-end pads. The Apex 5 is no exception, and I'd estimate that complaints about its quality – including squeaky buttons and creaking body – are slightly more frequent than others at this price point. But they're still rare, and if money were no object it's the pad I'd pick.
It's hard to go wrong for $20 – and the Ultimate 2c Wired gets a lot right. It feels sturdy in my hand, its Hall Effect sticks and triggers feel dependable, and it even has two extra programmable buttons.
It feels way better than $20 should. I remember growing up when $20 controllers would give up within weeks, bits falling off as their triggers groaned. The Ultimate 2C is different entirely: it feels like a well-built controller with comfortable curves that fill your palms. When I really try to twist it and warp it, I only get the measliest of creaks. It's reliable enough that some users keep it for years.
Its sturdy face buttons are reassuringly heavy. One of my main worries with budget pads is that mushy face buttons will quickly fail. 8BitDo's have some real heft to them, and depress with a weighty thud that gives me confidence they'll take a battering. It makes them a bit less spammable than other pads – my ShmupSpeed score was low – but on a budget pad, I take solid over fast every time.
Tight Hall Effect sticks shouldn't drift. Its sticks feel mobile: I had no problems aiming my gun, performing skill moves, or swinging the camera around on command. And because they're Hall Effect, rather than mechanical, they shouldn't succumb to "stick drift". That doesn't mean they won't loosen over time, though, and their centering error was towards the high end of what I tested. But that's expected given the price, and it's within the bounds of what's acceptable.
Its two extra buttons are easy to map. 8BitDo's software doesn't jive with the 2C wired, so you'll need to remap by holding down specific buttons on the controller itself. But that's fine, because it worked every time I tried it. The buttons themselves are just behind the bumpers, in a natural spot for your index fingers to find. I never accidentally pressed them – and they were there whenever I reached for them. Most budget pads won't have any extra buttons, so they feel like a bonus here.

The Cyclone 2 dock's barebones design means you have to place the controller in carefully, which is slightly annoying. But just by existing, it makes it more likely you'll charge the controller after a session – and that partially mitigates the average battery life of 6-10 hours. If you want to get as much juice out of it as possible, you can turn the RGB off and reduce the 1000Hz polling rate to 500Hz without taking any real noticeable hit in performance.

Its USB dongle connection is instant and reliable. I tested the GameSir in all three modes: wired, Bluetooth, and wireless via its USB dongle. The dongle is best – you'll find faster wireless connections on high-end pads, but the Cyclone 2 is still rapid, and I didn't notice any delay between my inputs and the in-game response. The dongle always recognised my controller instantly and the connection never dropped. Plus, I love how tiny the dongle is: you barely notice it sticking out of your PC or laptop, and you can store it in the charging dock for safekeeping.

Its crowd-pleasing shape will be comfortable for most people. Xbox's wireless controller is a tried and tested shape that fits most people, and the Cyclone 2's shape is nearly identical, down to the curve of the bumpers. I certainly found it comfortable to hold for hours at a time, no matter what genre I was playing, and my left thumb felt at home on its clicky D-Pad when playing Celeste. Whether you use one finger for the bumpers and triggers or two, you'll easily reach the two back buttons, one on each side of the controller.

GameSir's software all fits on one page. GameSir Connect controls the Cyclone 2, and I like that everything fits on a single screen. From there you can control RGB, change the polling rate, remap buttons, adjust the sticks and configure gyro controls. It's nothing revolutionary, but it feels streamlined.

It sticks aren't TMR but they feel better than anything I've ever used: tight, springy, and accurate, plus you can adjust the tension by removing the controller's face plate. All its buttons are solid and satisfyingly clicky, and its party trick is adaptive triggers that respond to your actions in games, ratcheting the tension up and down as you fire your gun or pulse the accelerator. A giant battery completes the package. It's $160, but it's worth it.

Its adaptive triggers are a genuine delight . In certain games, the triggers automatically adjust their tension to match your in-game actions: it's basically Flydigi's attempt to capture the joy of the Dualsense controller's triggers, and it's the best implementation you'll find outside of Sony's pad. It works in around 100 games and I enjoyed it most in GTA 5, where it changed when I was driving a car – increasing the resistance under braking or acceleration – or shooting a shotgun, which gave me a snap of breakthrough tension to mimic the gun firing, and then lots of recoil vibration. It's not perfect, and setting it up in FlyDigi's software isn't the most intuitive, but it genuinely makes games more fun. If your game is unsupported, you can still customize the trigger tension around five presets.

Sticks spring back to the center, and you can adjust the tension. These are, by far, the sticks I enjoyed the most. Not only are they smooth and responsive, but they fairly race back to dead center with a taught twang when you stop pushing them. They sit at dead center, with virtually zero deviation – their centering error was the lowest of the pads I tested. I also loved watching the mechanism twirl beneath the transparent face plate. On top of all that, you can adjust the tension. I wish it was easier: you have to first remove the faceplate and then twiddle a pair of tiny screws, but it's the kind of thing you can do once and then, when they're perfect for you, never do again.
